title: When does a workplace in Japan need safety and health managers and a safety and health committee?
description: Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act: safety and health manager thresholds, monthly committees, 3 year minutes and Article 19-2 capability training.
shortAnswer: Under Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act, a workplace with 50 or more regular workers must appoint a health manager and set up a health committee, and in listed industries also a safety manager and, at 50 or 100 workers, a safety committee. Committees meet at least monthly, deliberate on education plans and keep records for three years. Safety managers must complete a prescribed course, and Article 19-2 asks employers to provide ongoing capability training.
keyTakeaways: Article 12 and Article 4 of the Enforcement Order require a health manager at every workplace with 50 or more regular workers; Article 11 and Order Article 3 require a safety manager at that size in listed industries.
Health committees are required at 50 or more workers in all industries; safety committees at 50 or 100 workers depending on the industry (Order Articles 8 and 9).
Rule 23 of the Industrial Safety and Health Ordinance requires committees to meet at least monthly, publicize a summary to workers and keep records for three years.
Committees must deliberate on safety and health education plans (Rules 21 and 22), which gives them a formal role in the training program.

Article 19-2 sets an effort duty to provide capability improvement education for safety managers, health managers, promoters and others; failing to appoint managers or committees carries a fine of up to 500,000 yen.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), Prefectural Labor Bureaus and Labor Standards Inspection Offices
appliesTo: Employers with workplaces of 50 or more regular workers, in any industry, for health managers and health committees
Employers in listed industries such as manufacturing, construction, transport and utilities, for safety managers and safety committees
Workplaces of 10 to 49 workers, which appoint safety and health promoters or health promoters instead
Appointed safety managers, health managers, general safety and health managers and committee members
Workers' majority unions or representatives who nominate half the committee members

sections.heading: Which provisions set out the management structure?

blocks.text: Chapter 3 of the Industrial Safety and Health Act (Rōdō Anzen Eisei Hō, Act No. 57 of 1972) sets out the safety and health management structure, and Articles 17 to 19 add the committees. The thresholds are in the [Enforcement Order](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347CO0000000318) (Cabinet Order No. 318 of 1972) and the procedures in the [Industrial Safety and Health Ordinance](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/347M50002000032) (Ministry of Labor Ordinance No. 32 of 1972). As at November 2026, all provisions cited are the current e-Gov text.

This page covers appointments, committees and the capability training that supports them. Education for workers at hiring, for special hazardous work and for foremen is covered separately in [Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act training duties](/regulations/japan-industrial-safety-and-health-act-training).

sections.heading: Which managers must a workplace appoint?

blocks.text: The roles depend on headcount and industry. Workplaces are counted by the number of workers regularly employed (jōji shiyō suru rōdōsha) at each site.

blocks.caption: Management roles under the Industrial Safety and Health Act

blocks.text: Rules 2, 4 and 7 require appointment within 14 days of the obligation arising and an electronic report to the Labor Standards Inspection Office. Rule 7 sets the number of health managers by size, from one at 50 to 200 workers to six above 3,000. The [MHLW safety manager FAQ](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/koyou_roudou/roudoukijun/faq1.html) explains that a full time dedicated safety manager is required from 300 workers in construction and some chemical industries, 500 in others such as road freight, 1,000 in steel, paper and shipbuilding, and 2,000 elsewhere where over 100 workers were injured in three years.

sections.heading: What training must a safety manager complete before appointment?

blocks.text: A safety manager must have completed the training course set by the Minister of Health, Labour and Welfare, unless they are a labor safety consultant. Rule 5 sets this as part of the qualification, alongside a science education and years of industrial safety experience.

The MHLW FAQ calls this the safety manager appointment course (anzen kanrisha sen'nin ji kenshū) and lists the experience routes. A university or technical college science graduate needs 2 years of industrial safety experience; a high school science graduate needs 4; a non science university graduate needs 4; a non science high school graduate needs 6; and anyone else needs 7. Rule 4(3) requires the appointment report to be accompanied by electronic evidence that the person completed the course.

Health managers qualify mainly through a national license examination rather than a course. Safety and health promoters for smaller workplaces qualify through a course run by a body registered with the Prefectural Labor Bureau, as listed on the [MHLW qualifications and education page](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/roudoukijun/anzeneisei10/qualificaton_education.html).

sections.heading: When is a safety committee or health committee required?

blocks.text: A health committee is required at every workplace with 50 or more workers. A safety committee is required at 50 or more workers in higher risk industries and at 100 or more in the other industries that need a safety manager. An employer that needs both may set up a single safety and health committee under Article 19.

blocks.text: Article 17 requires the safety committee to deliberate on basic measures to prevent danger, on the causes of industrial accidents and recurrence prevention, and on other important matters. The chair is the general safety and health manager or the person who controls the business. Half the members other than the chair must be nominated on the recommendation of the majority union or, if none, the worker majority representative. The health committee must include the industrial physician and health managers.

sections.heading: How must committees operate, and what records are needed?

blocks.text: Rule 23 requires each committee to meet at least once a month. After each meeting the employer must promptly publicize a summary of the proceedings to workers by posting it in each workplace, handing out copies, or making an electronic file continuously available on a device in each workplace.

The employer must also record, for each meeting, the committee's opinions and the measures taken in response, and other important matters, and must keep that record for three years. Industrial physicians may ask the health committee or safety and health committee to deliberate on matters needed to protect workers' health.

Committees have a formal role in training. Rule 21(4) lists "preparing the implementation plan for safety education" among the important matters the safety committee must deliberate on, and Rule 22(4) does the same for health education in the health committee. Rule 22 also covers mental health measures and prevention of health harm from long working hours. The committee minutes are therefore a primary record of how the education plan was set and reviewed.

sections.heading: What does Article 19-2 require for capability improvement education?

blocks.text: Article 19-2(1) says that employers must endeavor to provide, or give opportunities to receive, education and training to improve the abilities of safety managers, health managers, safety and health promoters, health promoters and others engaged in preventing industrial accidents. It is an effort duty (doryoku gimu), not a strict duty with a penalty.

Article 19-2(2) requires the Minister to publish guidelines for this education, and Article 19-2(3) allows the Minister to give guidance to employers and their associations in line with those guidelines. Because the education is framed as raising the standard of safety and health at the workplace, it is best planned for each appointed person on a cycle, not delivered once at appointment.

The MHLW publishes a separate guideline under Article 60-2(3) for workers already engaged in dangerous or harmful work, revised most recently on May 25, 2026. That guideline is distinct from capability improvement education for managers but often runs through the same training calendar.

sections.heading: What are the penalties for not appointing managers or committees?

blocks.text: Article 120 of the Act makes it an offense, punishable by a fine of up to 500,000 yen, to breach Article 10(1), 11(1), 12(1), 17(1) or 18(1), among others. That covers failing to appoint a general safety and health manager, safety manager or health manager, and failing to establish a safety or health committee.

Article 11(2) also allows the chief of a Labor Standards Inspection Office to order an employer to increase the number of safety managers or replace one when necessary to prevent industrial accidents, and Article 12(2) applies the same power to health managers. Article 10(3) allows a Prefectural Labor Bureau director to make recommendations about how the general safety and health manager performs their role.

sections.heading: How should a multi site employer organize this?

items: Count regular workers at each site and map the site's industry to the Order Article 2, 3 and 8 categories.
List the roles and committees each site needs and the date each obligation arose.
Confirm that safety managers have completed the appointment course and hold the right experience, and that health managers hold the license class their industry requires.
Put the annual safety and health education plan on a committee agenda and record the deliberation.
Plan capability improvement education for each appointed person, with a refresh cycle.
Keep minutes and education records for at least three years, longer where internal policy requires.

blocks.text: [How to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix), [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) and [how to report training compliance to the board](/guides/how-to-report-training-compliance-to-the-board) cover the supporting mechanics. Employers in Japan should also align committee agendas with [heatstroke prevention duties](/regulations/japan-heatstroke-prevention-obligations), which committees commonly review before summer.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents each site with its industry and headcount, so the framework derives the managers and committees required and links each appointment to its qualification and capability training obligations. Committee minutes that approve the education plan become evidence attached to the plan's version, connecting governance decisions to the training that follows.

faqs.q: Does a health manager need a specific license class?
faqs.a: It depends on the industry. Rule 7 requires a first class health manager license, a health engineering health manager license or another listed qualification in industries such as agriculture, mining, construction, manufacturing, utilities, transport, vehicle and machine repair, medical care and cleaning. Other industries may also use a second class license holder.

faqs.q: Can committee meetings be held online?
faqs.a: Rule 23 requires monthly meetings and lets the committee decide its own operating rules beyond that, but it does not specify the format. Many employers hold meetings online. Whatever the format, the summary must be publicized to workers and the record of opinions and measures kept for three years.

faqs.q: Do workplaces with fewer than 50 workers need a committee?
faqs.a: No committee is required below 50 workers, though workplaces of 10 to 49 workers must appoint a safety and health promoter or health promoter under Article 12-2. Rule 23-2 also requires employers without a committee to create opportunities to hear the views of the workers concerned on safety and health matters.

faqs.q: Is capability improvement education legally mandatory?
faqs.a: Article 19-2 is an effort duty, so there is no fine for not providing it. However, the Minister can give guidance under Article 19-2(3), and a well documented program helps show that appointed managers can carry out the technical duties that Articles 11 and 12 require.
